Emberbrook — the camera-closeness round

Your redline: “the camera angle is often too high up and far away from the characters… they end up looking pretty small, like ants.” Left is what ships today. Right is the re-solved frame, drafted at 1008×576 / 28 spp with 1.7 m matte stand-ins on the shot’s own ground — nearest, middle and farthest point a player can stand. Draft renders are noisy by design; judge the framing, not the grain. The night grade is the shipped one, per shot, unchanged.

THE CLOSENESS BANDS, DERIVED 2026-08-02 (camera lane, closeness round). Every number
below is a measurement or a consequence of one; nothing here was chosen by taste.

1. THE INTERIOR BOUND, RE-MEASURED — AND THE OLD FIGURE IN THIS FILE WAS WRONG.
   Instrument: each interior blend opened in Blender, its own camera read, the 1.7 m
   figure projected at the far end of the WALKABLE floor (`walk_*` meshes only, head
   point, view-z — the same z the solver's charPxFar uses), frame 768 px tall.
        emb-inn-int      vfov 40   z_far 12.35 m   145 px
        emb-item-int     vfov 34   z_far 11.52 m   185 px
        emb-bakery-int   vfov 30   z_far 10.75 m   227 px
        emb-lake-int     vfov 26   z_far 11.41 m   248 px
   So the interiors run 145-248 px, median 206. THE 157-179 px RECORDED HERE ON THE
   MORNING OF 2026-08-02 IS VOID: it assumed a uniform vfov 35 that NOT ONE of the four
   interiors uses (they run 26-40), and it measured to the far WALL rather than to the
   far end of the floor a character can stand on. Both errors pushed it low.

2. ORDINARY TOWN SHOT: charPxFar 62-145 px.
   CEILING 145 = the loosest interior (the inn). The user's rule is that interiors are
   the upper bound on closeness, so no outdoor shot may read closer than the least-close
   interior. Nothing in this town is near it.
   FLOOR 62 IS THE MEASURED LIMIT OF THIS SHOT LIST, not a wish, and that distinction is
   the most important sentence in this note. charPxFar is bounded above by the region a
   shot owns: at any lens, charPxFar <= charH*768 / (2*E), where E is the half-extent the
   frame must hold. Festival Square is 32.7 x 28.7 m, so its ceiling is ~70 px at fov 0
   and 60 px at fov 14 — no angle and no lens reaches 80. Swept over 612 stands at five
   lenses, the worst ORDINARY shot's ceiling is gatefield at 65 px. 62 is set one notch
   under it, so the floor binds on the shot list rather than refusing it.

3. ESTABLISHING: charPxFar >= 40 px AND charPxNear >= 60 px.
   The near clause is the user's 'the player must still be easily visible': a shot the
   town is the subject of may lose the far corner, never the ground the player stands and
   talks on. ONE shot is designated establishing and it is `square` — Festival Square is
   the postcard of home, the frame Chapter One takes away, and it is measurably unable to
   meet the ordinary floor as one camera over a 33 m plaza (its own `_split_refused`
   records why a second camera in the plaza is refused by the WALK and not by the lens).
   `gateroad` was proposed as establishing this morning and IS NOT: it is a transit road
   with no town in it, it reaches 73 px, and it belongs in the ordinary band. A shot does
   not become establishing because it is hard to frame.

4. WHAT THIS ROUND COULD NOT REACH, recorded so the next one starts from the number.
   FF-parity closeness is about 15% of frame height, i.e. ~115 px at 768. This slate
   delivers a median 65 and a best 98. The gap is NOT a camera problem and cannot be
   re-aimed or re-lensed away: charPxFar <= charH*768/(2*E) makes it arithmetic about
   REGION SIZE. Emberbrook plays eleven shots over ~180 m; Dellhollow plays sixteen over
   ~100 m, i.e. this town is about 2.5x under-covered, and that under-coverage IS the
   ants complaint at its root. Reaching a 115 px floor town-wide needs roughly 18-22
   shots, which is a shot-list and seam-canon round (and, for the plaza, the map-topology
   fix `_split_refused` already names), not a framing pass.

The Whisperwood Road woodroad

THE GAME'S FIRST FRAME. The quiet road through the Whisperwood at dusk, looking north the way Vesper is walking: the arrival clearing behind her, the wood pressing close on both sides and closing the sky, the mossy waystone standing on the verge with EMBERBROOK cut into it, and the road climbing gently away past it toward a warmth that is not yet a village — no roof, no arch, no lamp in frame, only the light on the road. The village is a rumour until the next shot.

The Waystone waystone

The stone on the verge, and the second frame the game shows. Closer and lower than the clearing: the mossy marker standing off the road's west side with EMBERBROOK cut into it under the lichen and the hand-scratched note beneath that, the road going on past it up the last rise, and the wood still shoulder to shoulder on both sides. This is where Vesper's sketchbook and the waking world agree for the first time, and where Mochi hires himself.

The Village Arch arch

Arrival, and the game's first frame. From inside the village on the high west shoulder, looking back south down the road: the orchard rows falling away on the right with their ladders and baskets, the waystone on the bend, the timber arch and its harvest wreaths at the bottom of the road, and the valley the player has walked up beyond it. The road runs AWAY from camera, so the arch reads as a threshold you came through rather than a door you are about to open.

The Orchard Rows orchard

The harvest, and the only frame in the town that is WORK rather than home. Broadside across the rows from the road's own side: apple trees in ranks stepping away west with their ladders still against them and baskets under them, the open-sided cider press closing the frame with its crates and straw and the smell of the pressing, and the arch's lamp small back down the spur behind. Emberwake is the payoff of autumn and this is the ground it was grown on.

The Rise therise

THE REVEAL, and the only shot in the town whose subject is a thing that happens rather than a thing that stands. The climb from the arch up to the square, taken from off the road's west shoulder: the cobbles running up and away, the orchard's last rows falling behind on the left, and over the crest of the rise the village arriving one roof at a time — chimney smoke, then thatch, then the bunting, and the Heartlight's glow on the undersides of it all before the flame itself is in sight. Chapter One's beat 4 is walked here.

Festival Square squareestablishing

The postcard of home. Across the plaza from the north, with the Heartlight on its pedestal centre-frame and brightest — the inn's stone steps and lit windows to the right, the item shop and the notice board to the left, the bakery's warm window closing the west side, stalls and bunting around the ring, and the road running away south down the rise the player just climbed. This is the frame Chapter One takes away.

Pond Lane pondlane

The quiet one. Low along the shore looking back west up the lane, the pond filling the near half of frame with the Heartlight's glow lying on the water, the jetty's piles in silhouette, the plank footbridge over the brook mid-frame and the washing lines on the green to the right. Frogs, fireflies, and the last lamp of Lake's round out at the jetty.

Home Row homerow

Lake's round, first leg. Broadside to the home lane from below the rise, the cottages stepping up it west to east — Mara & Pip's at the junction, the keeper's cottage with its herbs over the door and the brass lighter inside, Rowan's ledgers at the top — the lane ending at the hilltop bench with the whole village and valley falling away behind. A lamppost at every door, and the brook running down between the row and the square.

The North Lane northlane

The walled climb. Side-on from over the pond, the lane running up the frame between its dry-stone walls from the square's north edge to the tithe barn, which is its landmark and its turn — cats in the rafters, harvest stores, and the back lane closed off with stacked Emberwake barrels. Above the barn the lane bends away east toward the gate court and the old edge of the village.

The Quiet Road gateroad

The middle of the seclusion, and the shot where the village leaves you. The road curving through the wood with the barn's roofline already gone behind the last bend and the gate not yet in front — seen from the outside of the curve and above it, so the road enters frame at one edge and leaves at the other and a player can read where it goes. No lamp, no fence, no cart, nothing anybody built. The environment shift the seclusion round was measured into the map: this is the stretch it happens ON.

The Old Gate gatefield

Chapter One's set-piece stage, and the only unwarm frame in the town. The flag-stoned court from the south, facing the sealed gate square-on with its twin sigil plates in the ground before it, and the Whisperwood trailhead with its stile on the court's west rim. Behind on the left is NOT the barn any more but the wood the quiet road came out of. No lamp reaches here — nobody's warmth does — and after the seclusion stamp (306554a) nothing else does either: the barn is 63 m back down a curving forest road, the village is out of sight from 16.6 m past it, and the court reads gray against a horizon of trees rather than against a village that is all lamplight. RE-AIM AT THE DISTRICT PASS: the framing below was solved against a court at (76,74), and the yaw note's reasoning — Pond Lane's crowns closing the due-south sightline — is about geometry 50 m away that this shot can no longer see.
